questions.why: $2.10. It closed above its open, so the top of the body is the close at $25.30. The upper shadow runs from there to the high at $27.40.
questions.lesson_line: Upper shadow is the high minus the top of the body. On a hollow candle, the top is the close.

questions.q: Open $60.00, high $60.10, low $57.00, close $59.40. How long is the lower shadow, in dollars?
questions.why: $2.40. It closed below its open, so it's a filled candle and the bottom of the body is the close at $59.40. The lower shadow runs down to the low at $57.00.
questions.lesson_line: On a filled candle the bottom of the body is the close. Measure the lower shadow from there.

questions.story: A stock has slid for a month. Today it opens at $22.00, rallies to $24.10, and fades to close at $22.50. The low is $21.90.
questions.q: Which word fits today's candle?
questions.why: Inverted hammer. Small body near the low, a long upper shadow, almost no lower shadow, and it came after a decline. The same candle after a rally would be a shooting star.
questions.lesson_line: After a decline, a long upper shadow shows buyers tried. They still need the next candle to prove it.

wrong.Shooting star: Same shape, but a shooting star forms after an advance. This one came after a month-long slide.
wrong.Hammer: A hammer's long shadow is below the body. This one's is above.
wrong.Gravestone doji: A gravestone has open, low and close together, with no real body. This one closed at $22.50 against a $22.00 open, so it has a real body.

conflicts: Hammer vs hanging man: ChartSchool (Introduction to Candlesticks) and Investopedia (Hanging Man) say the two look identical and are named by the trend before them; the body can be black or white. Fidelity's webinar slides (citing Kirkpatrick and Dahlquist) say they are 'differentiated by the color of the body' and that hammers have white bodies and shooting stars black ones. The unit follows ChartSchool and Investopedia (q22, q27, w2) and asks no question about the color of a hammer, hanging man, inverted hammer or shooting star.

Harami colors: ChartSchool's Pattern Dictionary and Glossary H, and Investopedia's Candlestick page, say the second candle is the opposite color. ChartSchool's reversal-pattern pages (citing Nison's Beyond Candlesticks) and Fidelity's slides say any color combination counts. No question asks a harami's colors (q33, q35, q38 rest only on body inside body).

Engulfing and the shadows: ChartSchool (Dictionary, bullish and bearish pages), Investopedia's Bullish Engulfing page and Fidelity's slides judge engulfing on the bodies only. Investopedia's Bearish Engulfing page says the body is what matters 'not the changes in the wicks', but its next takeaway also says 'the high must be higher and the low must be lower'. q28, q29 and q30 key the body-only definition the sources share; q29 asks whether every engulfing is an outside day (False), which holds under the majority definition. Checker, 2026-11-09: Investopedia's Bullish Engulfing page has the same split: it says the body is judged 'without regard to the length of the tail shadows', then describes the second day opening 'lower than the previous low' and closing 'higher than the previous high'. ChartSchool states outright that engulfing 'does not require the entire range (high and low) to be engulfed', so q29 stands.

Doji strictness: Fidelity's slides say a doji's open and close are 'the same price'. ChartSchool ('virtually equal', 'Ideally, but not necessarily') and Investopedia ('the same or very close to it'; dragonfly page: 'slight discrepancies') allow a small difference. q10 keys the looser rule, held by two publishers.

Candle color: ChartSchool, Investopedia (Real Body), CME and Schwab say the color compares the close with the same candle's open; CME adds 'depending on the color settings of your software' and Fidelity says 'most commonly'. Investopedia's Candlestick page (Bottom Line) says the color shows the close against 'the previous period'. Checker, 2026-11-09: StockCharts' own SharpCharts FAQ (s36) says its default draws a candle black or red by the prior day's close and hollow or filled by the open, so a gap up that fades but closes above the prior close is a filled black candle there. The fill rule is the same everywhere: q53 now keys the fill only (it said 'Filled (red)'), q15 asks the convention ('most charting platforms') and names the StockCharts exception, and w1 says 'most charts'.

Dark cloud cover open: ChartSchool says the black candle opens above the previous close; Schwab says above the previous high; Investopedia lists a gap up. q31's story opens above both the prior close and the prior high, so it qualifies under all three; q32 asks only for the midpoint, which all three agree on.

Shooting star gap: ChartSchool reports Greg Morris wants a gap up while Nison shows one without, and concludes 'the essence of the reversal should not be lost without the gap'. q24's story does not mention a gap and its key does not rest on one.

Star: Investopedia's Star page describes the small body appearing 'above the prior candle's range' (the evening-star case). ChartSchool says a star gaps up or down. q42 keys 'gaps away', which covers both, and cites both pages.

Bar vs candle: Schwab says the candlestick chart 'offers traders more information' than a bar chart. CME ('a bar chart provides four pieces of data ... the open, high, low and close'; 'Candlestick charts take the same information as a bar chart') and Fidelity agree the two carry the same four prices; Schwab's 'more' reads as the visual body and color. q54 keys the same-four-prices fact.

Three white soldiers: ChartSchool says each close should be near the high of the day; Investopedia says each close exceeds the previous candle's high. q47 keys only what both say: three long white candles in a row, each opening inside the prior body.

Marubozu: ChartSchool's Introduction and Investopedia define the full marubozu, with no upper or lower shadow. ChartSchool's Pattern Dictionary also counts a candle with no shadow at only one end (the open or the close). q19, q20 and q21 use the full version, which both publishers share.

Sources left out on purpose: Thomas Bulkowski's ThePatternSite.com states the site 'shall not be used to train artificial intelligence (AI) systems', and docs/study/TRAINING_CORPUS.md makes the whole Study module training material for UCT's own analysis system. To stay clear of that notice this unit cites no thepatternsite.com page; every key stands on ChartSchool, Investopedia, Schwab, Fidelity and CME. The owner may decide whether Bulkowski can be cited.
